title: Geo-fence and audit requirements intake with Orion Payments

Share Dedicated pricing and pilot SOW template

action_items: Maya Chen: Email SOC2, EU region matrix, and region-locking playbook by 2027-12-15

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-12
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Derek Patel, Sofia Ruiz (Redwood); James Rodriguez, Anika Bose, Tom Ellis, Priya Kaur (Orion Payments)

Summary: quick discovery focused on geo-fencing controls, audit trails, log residency and whether Redwood Hosted can satisfy EU financial regs; exploring Dedicated and Private options for controlled telemetry; agreed to exchange SOC2 and network diagrams and schedule a deeper technical session.

Topics: geo-fence / region-locking, log retention & redaction, KMS residency and escrow, SOC2/ISO evidence, network egress rules, SSO/SCIM, pilot timeline

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me today are Derek and Sofia from our solutions engineering team.
[00:08] James Rodriguez: Hi Maya, thanks. I'm James, head of platform at Orion. We have Anika, Tom and Priya here. We appreciate you making time.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Of course, quick round, objective for today is to understand your residency and audit constraints and map them to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options, and surface any blockers.
[00:27] Anika Bose: Great. High level, we're a payments processor with a pan-EU footprint. Our legal team is clear: no production PII or payment tokens can leave EU boundaries, and audit logs for payment flows must be retained in-region for seven years.
[00:41] Tom Ellis: Also network egress is heavily controlled. We use VPC peering and strict egress rules; any external call needs explicit firewall exception, and we prefer private endpoints when possible.
[00:52] Derek Patel: Got it. So two main axes: data residency for inference and for logs, plus network controls. Important to know if the redwood hosted offering has EU-only hosting regions with region-locking at the tenancy level.
[01:04] Maya Chen: Right. I can cover the product-level options briefly: Hosted supports region selection for models and an EU region with data processed in-region, but it has limited tenancy isolation compared to Dedicated. Dedicated gives reserved capacity in a customer-dedicated GPU pool, and Private is the full VPC/on-prem package with a private control plane.
[01:21] Priya Kaur: Quick clarification: when you say "region selection" for Hosted, does that guarantee logs never leave region? We have an internal auditor who will ask about incidental metadata, orchestration logs, and operator access.
[01:34] Sofia Ruiz: Good question. For Hosted we provide an EU region option where inference and token-level processing occur in-region, but some control-plane metadata (billing aggregates, usage metrics) may be replicated to our control plane for operational reasons. We offer tight contractual commitments and can limit replication — but for certain customers that's not sufficient.
[01:48] Anika Bose: That's the crux. Our compliance team treats any operator-level metadata as potential risk; we need to understand what those fields are and whether we can have them redacted or kept in-region.
[01:59] James Rodriguez: Also how do you handle log redaction and retention? We cannot store raw PANs or full card tokens in any log system outside of our vault.
[02:08] Derek Patel: We have a couple levers: prefix/KV cache can be configured to avoid persisting sensitive fields; you can send hashed or masked tokens, and we support log redaction and scrubbers at the ingestion layer. For Dedicated and Private, you control the storage endpoints and retention directly.
[02:22] Tom Ellis: Can you say more about KMS? Our keys must be EU-resident and under our control, preferably HSM-backed. If we go Dedicated, can we integrate our KMS?
[02:32] Maya Chen: Yes. Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS via cloud KMS integrations; Private supports bringing your own HSM/KMS entirely on-prem or in your VPC. For Hosted we manage keys, but there are enterprise options with bring-your-own-key in certain regions — subject to contract and HSM provider.
[02:47] Priya Kaur: And key escrow — do you provide an escrow mechanism? Our legal requires recoverability in case of disaster, but it must remain in EU.
[02:55] Derek Patel: For Private we can implement customer-controlled escrow processes, or we can integrate with your chosen escrow vendor. For Dedicated, we usually negotiate KMS key policies that keep master keys in your account or a customer-controlled HSM.
[03:07] Anika Bose: Okay. What about audit trail evidence? We need immutable logs, signed, and exportable for regulatory review. Do you provide append-only logs with tamper evidence?
[03:17] Sofia Ruiz: We provide audit logs with timestamps, request IDs, and operator access events. For Hosted, logs are stored in our managed logging stack; we can provide certified extracts, and for enterprise customers we can do longer retention and signed exports. For Private and Dedicated you host the log storage, so you can put them into an append-only store with your signing process.
[03:34] James Rodriguez: Does Redwood support export of logs to customer-owned S3 in EU? That would be ideal so we can attach Lifecyle policies and set retention.
[03:42] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated and Private can push logs to customer-owned S3 endpoints. Hosted can forward logs but whether it goes to a customer bucket depends on the contract and integration work. We can walk through a connector.
[03:53] Tom Ellis: One more on access: can you restrict Redwood operator access to production namespaces? We need RBAC enforced and require emergency access to be logged and approved.
[04:02] Derek Patel: We have role-based access controls and can enforce least privilege. For Hosted, operator access is tightly controlled and audited; emergency access requires approval from both the operations and security teams and is logged. For Dedicated and Private, you get more control — especially Private where the control plane can be customer-managed.
[04:16] Priya Kaur: About PII in prompts — we have an ingestion tier that normalizes records but inevitably some prompts may contain user-identifying info. Can Redwood help with dynamic redaction or pattern matching on tokens?
[04:27] Sofia Ruiz: Yes, we support customizable pre-processing hooks where you can run regex-based scrubbing, tokenization, and redaction before data hits the model. This runs in your environment for Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we offer server-side scrubbers with a set of rules you can configure.
[04:40] Anika Bose: How do you handle regulatory hold and legal e-discovery? If a regulator asks for all interactions for a user, how easily retrievable is that?
[04:49] Derek Patel: We tag requests with IDs and store trace metadata. For Dedicated/Private you can retain full payloads per your policies. For Hosted, we can provide exports but by default we advise pushing critical logs to customer-owned storage for legal holds.
[04:59] James Rodriguez: Let's talk about network topology for a minute. Our security team will only allow calls to known IP ranges and needs TLS mutual auth for service-to-service. Can Redwood support mTLS and fixed IP ranges?
[05:09] Maya Chen: Yes. Private supports mTLS and static IP egress; Dedicated can provide static egress IPs for integration. Hosted can support allow-listing but static IP guarantees are more challenging; we can discuss reserved network paths.
[05:22] Tom Ellis: What about data residency for intermediate artifacts — embeddings, cache layers, and checkpointing? We use embeddings for dedup and similarity on tokenized payloads, and cannot have those vectors leaving EU.
[05:33] Derek Patel: We can pin model artifacts and caches to EU nodes. Embedding vectors and caches are stored in-region for Dedicated/Private; for Hosted we document the store locations and if needed can provide region-only operation. There is a caveat: some multi-region control-plane metadata may reference request IDs, but the vectors and model states remain in-region when configured.
[05:48] Anika Bose: You mentioned operator logs earlier — are those subject to GDPR requests? How do you process subject access requests that reference logs?
[05:56] Sofia Ruiz: Logs that contain PII are redacted by default. For GDPR SARs, we have legal processes and can help generate exports; we strongly recommend keeping customer-identifiable logs in customer-owned storage to avoid joint liability and to simplify SAR response.
[06:10] Priya Kaur: On the encryption front, at-rest and in-flight is a given, but do you support field-level encryption in transit so that certain fields never appear in plaintext within Redwood's systems?
[06:20] Derek Patel: Field-level encryption can be implemented at the client side; Redwood integrates with client-side encryption patterns. For scenarios needing that guarantee, Private is the best fit, but we can design a hybrid where sensitive fields are encrypted client-side and Redwood never sees them.
[06:33] James Rodriguez: What SLA and uptime do you offer for Dedicated? Our SLAs require 99.95% for inference critical paths.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Our Dedicated contracts include SLA tiers; 99.95% is available on higher tiers with reserved capacity and failover zones. We can include latency SLOs per model profile as well.
[06:51] Tom Ellis: A bit more on proof: our audit team requires attestations and technical evidence — runbooks for failover, proof of region lock, and a list of subprocesses that might touch data. Can you deliver that level of operational detail?
[07:02] Sofia Ruiz: Yes — for enterprise customers we provide runbooks, architecture diagrams, list of processes, and operator access logs. Some details are redacted for security, but we can provide sufficient artifacts for auditors.
[07:12] Anika Bose: We saw you in a benchmark with other vendors — there were notes about batching improving cost but potentially increasing tail latency. We need low tail latency for authorizations. How does Redwood balance this?
[07:23] Derek Patel: We expose batching controls and dynamic batching policies. For auth flows you can pin models to low-batch strict latency paths or enable tiny batch sizes. Dedicated gives you the deterministic throughput to avoid tail latency increases; Hosted has smart batching to balance cost and latency but for strict auth use we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[07:40] James Rodriguez: Can you do a pilot with a subset of traffic in EU-only and show us tail latency numbers under our load profile?
[07:46] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Typical pilot is a 4-week PoC with dedicated capacity in EU — we can set up a canary route for a percentage of traffic, run benchmarks, and produce a report.
[07:55] Priya Kaur: Timeline wise, we need procurement and security sign-off before January end. If we start a PoC mid-December it helps, but procurement cycles are slow.
[08:04] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll aim to get SOC2 docs and an SOW out this week to accelerate procurement.
[08:11] Tom Ellis: A few nitty-gritty questions: can we rotate keys without downtime? How are KV caches invalidated across nodes?
[08:19] Derek Patel: Key rotation designed with zero-downtime—we support key rotation with rolling re-encrypt and dual-key windows. KV cache invalidation uses versioned keys and tombstones; for Private you control garbage collection windows.
[08:31] James Rodriguez: Any limitations on throughput for geo-fenced clusters? We sometimes burst for month end.
[08:38] Maya Chen: Dedicated supports predictable autoscaling and burst capacity options; for extreme burst you can pre-warm capacity. Private can be sized to your needs but depends on your infra.
[08:47] Anika Bose: Let's talk about evidence for auditors: for example, how would you prove to a regulator that requests originating from EU never left EU?
[08:55] Sofia Ruiz: Through a mix of network flow logs, signed audit exports, and infrastructure diagrams showing region-isolated subnets and inability to route traffic outside. For Dedicated and Private we can provide network ACL configs, flow logs, and signed attestations.
[09:09] Tom Ellis: We also use a GDPR data map — could Redwood provide a data classification mapping for the types of data and where they are stored?
[09:16] Derek Patel: Yes, we can provide a data map describing which artifacts are ephemeral, which are persisted, retention windows, and default store locations. We'll add that to the deliverables.
[09:25] James Rodriguez: Another practical ask — can we have a list of the exact AWS regions and AZs you use in EU for Hosted? Our procurement needs those exact names.
[09:33] Maya Chen: We'll provide the exact region names and pool endpoints in the follow-up doc. For Dedicated/Private we'll give you full endpoint addresses.
[09:40] Priya Kaur: One red flag for us is vendor operator access. Could you explain the approval path for emergency access and if we can have a joint custodian model?
[09:48] Sofia Ruiz: Emergency access requires dual approvals, is time-limited, and is fully audited. We can accommodate a joint custodian model where your on-call is involved in the approval flow.
[09:58] Anika Bose: Good. On the legal front, our counsel will want indemnities and data processing addendum language specific to financial services. Is that standard in your enterprise agreements?
[10:07] Maya Chen: Yes, we have an enterprise DPA and can negotiate sector-specific clauses for financial customers. We'll flag this for legal.
[10:14] Tom Ellis: For the PoC, what instrumentation will you need from our side? SDKs, sample traffic, TL;DR?
[10:20] Derek Patel: We'll need a sample traffic replay or live canary, API keys scoped to the PoC, and a lightweight sidecar or proxy to enforce any field-level scrubbing you want. We'll provide the SDKs and example configs.
[10:31] James Rodriguez: About costs — can you give a typical ballpark for a 4-week Dedicated pilot in EU with reserved minimal capacity? We need a rough number today for budgeting.
[10:39] Maya Chen: Ballpark for a basic Dedicated pilot with reserved nodes and telemetry forwarding is X to Yk per month — I'll avoid hard numbers on the call but will send a tailored estimate in the SOW.
[10:48] Priya Kaur: Please, include costs for optional managed KMS and extended log retention in that estimate.
[10:53] Maya Chen: Noted.
[10:55] Anika Bose: One last security thing: we require periodic penetration tests and a remediations timeline. Do you run pentests and share reports?
[11:03] Sofia Ruiz: We run yearly pentests and can share high-level summaries; we provide SOC2 Type II reports and can discuss sharing redacted pentest evidence under NDA.
[11:13] James Rodriguez: Great. Can we recap next steps?
[11:17] Maya Chen: Sure. Recap: 1) Redwood to send SOC2, EU region hosting matrix, and preliminary SOW by 2027-12-15. 2) SE team to prepare network diagram and PoC config for Private/Dedicated by 2027-12-19. 3) Orion to share data flow diagram and a list of endpoints to be geo-fenced by 2027-12-16. 4) Schedule a 2-hour technical deep dive week of 2027-12-20.
[11:42] Tom Ellis: Sounds good. We'll try to get the data map over this week.
[11:46] Maya Chen: Perfect — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Thanks everyone.
[11:52] Anika Bose: Thanks all.
[11:54] James Rodriguez: Appreciate it.

End of transcript.
